chunks: Debugging a microcontroller: hardware vs software. The question: How do you debug a microcontroller? What are some challenges at hardware vs software levels?
When a microcontroller board misbehaves, first decide whether the fault is in the hardware or in the software, because they need different tools. Work from the bottom up.
Check power, clock and reset first, then connect a debugger and look at the code. Change one thing at a time and write down what you saw.
Your car will not start. A sensible mechanic checks the battery and the fuel before blaming the driver's technique.
Only when the basics are fine does the mechanic look at finer problems. A board is the same.
If the power supply sags, no amount of code fixing will help, and you would waste hours looking in the wrong place.
A top-down symptom is investigated bottom-up. Each diamond is a cheap test that eliminates a whole layer; stop at the first "no" and fix that layer before going further.
Debugger: ("What a debugger is"): a tool that lets you halt the running program and inspect it.
Breakpoint: a marker that stops the program at a chosen line so you can look around. Oscilloscope: an instrument that shows a voltage over time, so you can see dips and noise.
Logic analyzer: an instrument that records many digital signals at once and can decode a bus such as I2C or SPI.
Brown-out: the supply voltage dipping low enough to reset or upset the chip.
A board keeps restarting at random. You put an oscilloscope on the 3. 3 volts supply. Every time a motor switches on, the supply dips to about 2.
4 volts for a moment, which is low enough to reset the chip. That is a hardware problem, such as a missing capacitor. Reading the code line by line would never find it.
If the supply is steady, you move up a layer and connect the debugger. That is the whole idea.
"I partition the problem. First check hardware basics with a multimeter and scope: power rails, clock, reset and boot pins.
Then connect a debugger over SWD or JTAG to halt, step, and inspect registers and memory.
For timing-sensitive bugs I use non-intrusive tools: GPIO toggles on a scope, a logic analyzer on buses, or trace.
Challenges are intermittent hardware faults, probes disturbing circuits, and real-time software bugs like interrupt races that vanish when halted."
